Fit a Stan MAP prior generation model to historical patient-level data.

Source: R/stan_map_patient_data.R
stan_map_patient_data.Rd

Fit a Stan MAP prior generation model to historical patient-level data.

Usage

stan_map_patient_data(y, trial, time, a_alpha, a_beta, b_alpha, b_beta, ...)

Arguments

y

integer vector, 0 for no event, 1 for event, for all patients.

trial

integer vector, denoting which trials patients belong to.

time

numeric vector, strictly positive, times at risk for patients.

a_alpha

numeric, first shape param of beta prior on a. See Details.

a_beta

numeric, second shape param of beta prior on a. See Details.

b_alpha

numeric, first shape param of beta prior on b. See Details.

b_beta

numeric, second shape param of beta prior on b. See Details.

...

extra parameters are passed to sampling.

Value

object of type bssd_binary_map.

Details

This routine fits the meta-analytical model equation: $$ log(-log(1 - p_{ij})) = \alpha_{j} + log(T_{ij}) $$ where \(p_{ij}\) is the probability of event in trial j, adjusted for the time-at-risk of patient i, \(T_{ij}\). The model is equivalent to: $$ log(\lambda_{ij}) = \alpha_{j} $$ where $$ \lambda_{ij} = -log(1 - p_{j}) / T_{ij} $$ is the hazard of the event, assumed constant through time, and \(p_{j}\) is the probability of event in unit time in trial j. Thus this is a random-effects model that assumes the log-hazard terms are exchangeable across trials, and the \( \alpha_{j} \) terms are trial-specific intercepts. To complete the meta-analytical model, we apply the hierarchical distribution $$ p_{j} \sim Beta(abN, (1-a)bN)$$ where N is the total number of patients in the historical trials, and a and b are hyperparameters. To illustrate the role of a and b, consider that the effective sample size of this distribution is \(abN + (1-a)bN) = bN\), i.e. b is a discount to the historical data, taking values on (0, 1). Furthermore, the mean of this distribution is \( abN / bN = a\). Thus, a is the expected probability of event in unit time, and once again a is bound to the range (0, 1). Hyperpriors \( a \sim Beta(a_{\alpha}, a_{\beta}) \) and \( b \sim Beta(b_{\alpha}, b_{\beta}) \) are natural choices to enforce these ranges. If you do not have patient-level times-at-risk and adverse event statuses, stan_map_summary_data provides a similar method to create a prior from summary-level data, requiring only the intended or average times-at-risk and total counts of patients with the event in each trial. It is likely aggregate statistics like this can be derived from publications and/or filings. The patient-level approach is generally preferable, however, because it allows adjustment for how long each individual patient spent at risk.

Note: setting a seed in R does not affect the state of the random generator in stan. If a reproducible output is desired, then the optional parameter seed needs to be populated. For additional information about this parameter, see sampling.

Examples

# Use a short MCMC run for this illustrative example.
check_iter <- 500
check_chains <- 1
set.seed(2021)
N <- 100
time <- 0.5 + cumsum(rexp(N, 100))
# Use constant hazard model:
hazard <- 0.15
prob <- 1 - exp(- hazard * time)
y <- rbinom(N, size = 1, prob = prob)
trial <- sample(1:5, size = N, replace = TRUE)
x <- stan_map_patient_data(y = y, trial = trial, time = time,
                           a_alpha = 1 / 3, a_beta = 1 / 3,
                           b_alpha = 5, b_beta = 5,
                           iter = check_iter, chains = check_chains,
                           refresh = 0)
#> Warning: Bulk Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior means and medians may be unreliable.
#> Running the chains for more iterations may help. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#bulk-ess
#> Warning: Tail Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior variances and tail quantiles may be unreliable.
#> Running the chains for more iterations may help. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#tail-ess
x
#> Prob(Event): Mean 0.117 (95% HPDI 0.05, 0.188)
#> MAP Prob(Event): Mean 0.123 (95% HPDI 0.02, 0.245)
